definition: Credulity means a readiness to believe things without proof.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word credulity. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know credulity should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Online quizzes that promise to reveal your true personality thrive on the credulity of readers who never ask how a dozen questions could know them.
Trust is usually earned by a person's track record; credulity goes further, handing out belief before any record exists.
Gullibility goes a step past credulity: the credulous believe too easily, while the gullible actually get taken in and duped by it.

Trustfulness is a warm readiness to rely on people - you assume your neighbor, your teammate, your doctor means well. Credulity aims at claims rather than people: swallowing the statement itself, however unlikely, without asking for proof. You trust a person; credulity accepts a story.

Naivety is broad inexperience of how the world works, and it shows everywhere - overpaying, oversharing, missing the joke. Credulity is one narrow habit inside that territory: accepting claims without demanding evidence. A naive person may misjudge anything; credulity specifically believes too easily.

Faith is belief held without proof on purpose - a chosen, often deeply considered commitment to a person, a cause, or a religion. Credulity is not chosen at all: it is the unthinking habit of believing whatever comes along, because asking for evidence never occurs to you.

Credulity means a readiness to believe things without proof.
When the text message claimed her streaming account was locked and a small fee would restore it, Gran typed in her card number without a moment's doubt.
It was not foolishness - she was sharp at cards and crosswords - but a lifetime of trusting official-looking letters had left her with a credulity that scammers count on.
Credulity is not the same as stupidity, and it is not quite trust either.
It names one specific habit: accepting claims without asking for proof.
Gran's mind is quick; what she lacks is the reflex to demand evidence before believing.
Credulity is the writer's word for believing too easily; it judges the habit, not the person's intelligence.
Gullibility is blunter and more insulting - it implies someone will be fooled.
Say a scam 'preys on credulity' in an essay; tell a friend they are 'too trusting' to their face.

In August 1835, the New York Sun began publishing what it called astronomical discoveries: forests on the moon, herds of lunar bison, and man-bats building temples.
The articles cited a famous astronomer and a telescope of impossible power.
Neither the astronomer nor the telescope had anything to do with it.
Readers debated the man-bats over breakfast; almost no one asked how any telescope could see a flower at that distance.
The Sun never quite apologized.
One editor observed, cheerfully, that the paper had merely measured the public's credulity and found it bottomless.
Historians note the sting in that word: the readers were not fools in general, and most trusted their neighbors no more than usual.
They had simply accepted an astonishing story without asking for proof.
